source.title: Where Causal Attention Cannot Reach: Localizing Refusal in Masked Diffusion Language Models

record.tranche_reason: Applies the original contrastive mean-difference extraction and residual-stream projection/addition interventions to masked diffusion language models, then measures refusal outcomes.
record.gate_note: The paper reports validation-set sweeps used to select source layers and token positions; those selection values are not separately recorded as outcome rows. Comparisons for GCG, PAIR, Slice, PAD, and DIJA are not included as rows here because they are other methods, not results of the refusal direction itself. Cited attack results from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study applies Arditi et al.'s difference-in-means extraction, unchanged, to three masked diffusion LMs, a new architecture. It measures refusal under projection-based removal and activation addition with the original measures (keyword refusal, LLaMA-Guard 2) plus StrongREJECT. It also tests English–Chinese transfer. This is a new setting with direct results on V1 and V6, so T3 rather than T1.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors frame the main contribution as localization, not the existence of a direction. Refusal is decodable and steerable at pre-instruction template tokens, is fully formed in the prompt-only pass, and acts mainly at the first denoising step. Bidirectional control is claimed for LLaDA-8B-Instruct and LLaDA-1.5 only. On MMaDA, steering is weaker on LLaMA-Guard, which they attribute to diffuse localization. They report English–Chinese transfer and do not claim to exhaust refusal structure.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the original contrastive mean-difference extraction and projection/addition ideas, but adapts them to masked diffusion. The selected direction is applied globally across layers, positions, and denoising steps; extraction sites and timing are studied in this non-causal architecture.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by model (MMaDA versus the two LLaDA variants), source position (pre- versus post-instruction), extraction time (prompt-only versus denoising steps), intervention schedule, token segment, and layer range.

fits_no_version.finding: A logistic probe at a pre-instruction template token (layer 17) classifies harmful vs benign prompts at AUROC 0.973, against 0.508 for random-label controls.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In non-causal MDLMs, harmfulness information is linearly decodable at chat-template tokens that precede the instruction.

fits_no_version.finding: Mean-difference sentiment directions, extracted in the prompt pass (including pre-instruction sources), steer sentiment bidirectionally on all three MDLMs. This includes MMaDA, where refusal steering was weak.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prompt-pass, pre-instruction localization of steerable directions in MDLMs extends beyond refusal.

record.problems: The paper evaluates three MDLMs and one main refusal benchmark; the text notes that broader model, architecture, scale, and alignment-recipe coverage is needed. MMaDA has weak baseline refusal and mixed intervention outcomes. General capabilities are not evaluated, and the authors say their directions need not exhaust refusal structure. Some timing and localization results are presented only in figures; Table 2 reports mean ± standard deviation across 3 seeds where applicable.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: Whether general capabilities are preserved under ablation; no capability benchmark is run.
No weight-edit or abliteration is tested; all interventions are at inference time.
No test of whether jailbreaks act via the direction, and no adversarial training against its ablation.
There is no single-direction vs multi-direction or cone comparison. The authors say their directions need not exhaust refusal structure.
Not separated: the probe decodes harmfulness but is not contrasted with the refusal decision.
Only English↔Chinese language transfer is tested. There is no transfer across model variants or from base to instruct.
Training is not manipulated. The paper only notes that MMaDA's diffuse localization differs from the LLaDA models.

missing.what: Keyword refusal of 38% when steering at layer 23 only, and the other layer-range values (e.g. late 25–32, 9–24), shown in the figure but not recorded
Refusal-induction source-site sweep: induction localized to layers 21–27 and trailing post-instruction tokens
StrongREJECT convincingness and specificity under removal (e.g. LLaDA-8B Post 3.31/3.38 vs Direct 1.13/1.14), which show the outputs are substantive rather than just refusal-free

record.verdict_notes: The global removal used here projects the direction out at all layers, positions and steps, as in Arditi's ablation; addition is applied at the source layer only. Row r25 and rows r47–r50 lack model names in their tables; the context points to LLaDA-8B-Instruct. MMaDA's low baseline refusal means the V1 premise (a model that refuses) is weakly met. Its contrary LLaMA-Guard and StrongREJECT moves are therefore treated as limits_scope, not challenges. The tranche could be argued as T1, since the procedure is unchanged, but the architecture is new.

versions.untested_parts: Whether general capabilities remain largely intact; the study does not evaluate general capability. It tests activation-space projection and addition, not weight edits.
No weight-edit or released-model abliteration procedure is tested.
The study does not test whether jailbreaks suppress this direction or whether training against its ablation adds robustness.

The study shows that a selected direction can steer refusal but does not compare a single direction with an affine subspace, cone, or multiple-direction account. It explicitly does not claim to exhaust refusal structure.
It probes harmful-versus-benign classification but does not separate harmfulness judgment from the refusal decision.
Transfer is tested between English and Chinese on one LLaDA setting; transfer across model variants or from base to instruct models is not tested.
The paper compares models with differing alignment regimes but does not manipulate when or how refusal training occurs.

relationships.condition: LLaDA-8B-Instruct and LLaDA-1.5, global removal with prompt-pass direction (pre- or post-instruction source); addition on benign prompts
relationships.reason: Removal cuts keyword refusal from 95–96% to 0–5%, with LLaMA-Guard dropping about 78–80 points and StrongREJECT score rising (r1–r16, r28, r40, r43, r45). Addition induces refusal on 89% of benign prompts (r25).
relationships.display_finding: Removal reduced keyword refusal from 95–96% to 0–5%, lowered LLaMA-Guard refusal by about 78–80 points, and raised StrongREJECT scores; addition induced refusal on 89% of benign prompts.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: LLaDA-8B-Instruct and LLaDA-1.5, global removal with prompt-pass direction (pre- or post-instruction source); addition on benign prompts
source_check.reason: Table 2: keyword 95.0–96.3% to 0–5%, LLaMA-Guard 2 down 78–80 points, StrongREJECT score 0.02–0.04 to 0.49–0.61. Addition takes keyword refusal from 2% to 89% (Table 3; model not named, likely LLaDA-8B-Instruct). Capability was not measured, so that part of V1 is untested, not limited.

relationships.reason: Keyword and StrongREJECT refusal fall only modestly (r17, r19, r21, r23). LLaMA-Guard safety rises (14.3% to 22–26%) and StrongREJECT score falls (0.45 to 0.29), opposite to suppression (r18, r20, r22, r24). The authors attribute this to diffuse localization.
relationships.display_finding: Keyword and StrongREJECT refusal decreased modestly, but LLaMA-Guard safety rose from 14.3% to 22–26% and the StrongREJECT score fell from 0.45 to 0.29.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: Table 2: keyword 10.7% to 4–5% and SR refusal 12.0% to 7.0–8.7% (right direction, from a low base). LLaMA-Guard safety rises 14.3% to 22–26% and SR score falls 0.45 to 0.29. Mixed measures on a weakly refusing model qualify V1 rather than show it absent; authors attribute it to diffuse localization.

relationships.condition: LLaDA-8B-Instruct, varying extraction time, intervention steps, token segment, and layer range
relationships.reason: Directions extracted at denoising steps are weak (87–98% safety; r29–r33). Late-only steps (r35) and output-only tokens (r39, r42) are inert or near it. Early layers have no effect (r46). The extraction layer alone reaches only 68% (r44), and input-only only 68%/54% (r38, r41). The effect depends on extraction and intervention choices.
relationships.display_finding: Denoising-step directions left 87–98% safety, while late steps, output tokens, and early layers had little or no effect; extraction-layer-only intervention left 68% safety and input-only interventions left 68% or 54%.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: LLaDA-8B-Instruct, varying extraction time, intervention steps, token segment, and layer range
source_check.reason: Fig. 2: step-conditioned directions give 87–98% safety against 18% for prompt-only. A.8: output-only 91%, layer 23 alone 68%, input-only 68%, layers 1–8/1–16 near baseline. The effect depends on extraction time and intervention layers. The token and layer restrictions are partial ablations Arditi did not use.

relationships.reason: An English-extracted direction cuts Chinese keyword refusal from 97% to 1% and LLaMA-Guard from 99% to 31%. A Chinese-extracted direction cuts English refusal from 86% to 3% and LLaMA-Guard from 100% to 9% (r47–r50).
relationships.display_finding: The English direction reduced Chinese keyword refusal from 97% to 1% and LLaMA-Guard safety from 99% to 31%, while the Chinese direction reduced English refusal from 86% to 3% and safety from 100% to 9%.

The result is from LLaDA-8B-Instruct only, not 'diffusion LMs' in general.
